newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Uncertainty surrounds Roche H1 forecasts. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Uncertainty surrounds Roche H1 forecasts. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: An air of uncertainty surrounds forecasts for Roche Holding AG these days as analysts grapple with the impact of new drug launches and the largest acquisition in the history of the Swiss pharmaceuticals group.
But beneath this uncertainty, momentum seems to be building in Roche's non-voting equity securities, or certificates, ahead of the new phase of earnings growth expected to arrive in 1998.
"I believe these numbers are a watershed as Roche marks the end the transition years," said Peter McDougall of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

But for now, Roche remains in transition and analysts are not expecting full clarity until next year when earnings from new drug sales come on stream and the impact of the $11 billion takeover of the German-based Boehringer Mannheim group is clear.
On average, analysts expect Roche on Friday to report a 10.9 percent rise in first-half group net profit to 2.45 billion Swiss francs ($1.6 billion) with forecasts ranging from 2.05 to 2.75 billion.
"There is a lot of uncertainty and the six-month figures are hard to forecast because of the marketing expenditure," said Beat Alpiger of Bank Julius Baer.

Overall, analysts are looking at the first-half earnings report as largely a "non-event" with operating profits squeezed by heavy marketing spending, but financial income boosted by the recent stellar performance by equity markets.
"Roche has been talking down its numbers since the beginning of the year," said Richard Vietor of Merrill Lynch Global Securities Research.

Roche regards 1996 and 1997 as transition years with profits under pressure from product developments and the hiring of an additional 1,000 sales people in the U.S. alone, mainly to push the sales of the Posicor and Xenical drugs, both viewed as very promising by Roche and analysts.
"The costs are high, but so far there is no revenue," said Birgit Kulhoff of Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
Roche, traditionally strong in the hospital market, hired the additional sales force as both drugs takes it into the outpatient market, a relatively new terrain for Roche.

In addition to the impact of these new drugs, analysts are also grappling with the effect of Roche's purchase of Boehringer Mannheim, a move that not only dilutes first-year earnings, but also radically change its future earnings profile.

In the past financial income from Roche's cash pile of 15 billion francs was a significant chunk of net profit. In 1996 for example financial income made up one-third of net profit. But financing the acquisition will sharply reduce Roche's cash pile and thus its financial income stream.

"By year 1999/2000 Roche will almost have no net financial income because of debt payments and Genentech," said Marc Becker of J.P. Morgan (corrects from SBC Warburg), referring to Roche's option to complete the purchase of U.S. biotech company Genentech in 1999.

The initial effect of the Boehringer Mannheim acquisition is that Roche will take a restructuring charge, which could be reach one billion francs, analysts estimate. The burning question is when Roche will take this charge and consolidate Boeringer Mannheim. Only the authorities, who have to approve the acquisition, can provide the answer.

Question marks about Boeringer Mannheim and new drugs are likely to dampen short-term performance of Roche certificates, which have underperformed the SPI index ever since they were hit by the one-two punch of the birth of Novartis in early 1996 and the onset of a two-year phase of slow growth.

These questions are mirrored in analysts' 1997 and 1998 forecasts. On average 1997 forecast look for a net profit of 4.18 billion francs, but the range is from 3.7 billion to 4.5 billion francs, depending on when charges are taken.
Profit forecast for 1998 average 5.03 billion francs with a range from 4.35 billion to 5.4 billion.
"At the end of the day, all these issues are rather academic because the stock is going up," said McDougall.
There is growing evidence that Roche certificates may be on the verge of taking off and the first-half results might just add a little more fuel to the expected liftoff.
Since July 1 Roche's non-voting equity securities, or certificates have risen 7.0 percent compared with a fall of 0.8 percent for Novartis, noted J.P. Morgan's (corrects from SBC Warburg's) Becker.
But opinions over when market sentiment will finally shift toward Roche certificates is strongly divided.

The most sceptical analysts first expect an upturn in the second half of 1998, when Roche's earnings start growing from the sales of Posicor and Xenical. But other analysts doubt the market will wait so long.

Merrill's Vietor and J.P. Morgan's (corrects from SBC Warburg's) Becker are looking for the certificates to react in October, when Roche's third-quarter sales figures begin to show the first effects of Posicor, which was launched in July.
"The certificates will be be driven by the revenue story," said Vietor.
-- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
($ = 1.526 Swiss Francs)
